Flash remediation — Phase 1: synthetic characterization

FoV-truncation artifacts in mbirjax MBIR recon · 2026-07-08 · plan of record: plans/flash_remediation/flash_remediation_plan.md · scripts: plans/experiments/flash_remediation/

TL;DR. Both flash artifacts (the radial ring and the SiC-like axial flash + z-ringing) reproduce on small synthetic cone-beam cases, and both are confirmed to be model-support problems: enlarging the reconstruction support with the existing scale_recon_shape() essentially eliminates them.

Radial (object wider than the FoV): padding improves the RoR-edge ring 37× and the interior 2.8× — lateral truncation biases the entire interior, which no channel weight taper can reach.

Axial, one-sided (object taller than the covered slab): padding improves the truncated-end slices 9× and removes the z-ringing; the artifact is localized, and grows with iterations if unaddressed.

1  The two truncation cases at a glance

MBIR explains the measured attenuation with the voxels of the reconstruction support. When part of the scanned object lies outside that support, the data term is inconsistent: some measured attenuation has no voxels that can account for it. The optimizer deposits that unexplained attenuation in the least-constrained voxels available — the ones at the support boundary — producing the bright “flash.” The two ways an object can leave the support behave differently, and the distinction drives the remediation choice.

Radial (channel) truncation — top view

The object is wider than the FoV. As the gantry rotates, material at radius r beyond the FoV sweeps across every channel |c| ≤ r — the inconsistency lands throughout the sinogram, not just at the edge channels. Artifact: bright ring at the RoR boundary plus a positive bias over the whole interior. Seen in: z62 (partition study), the BGA scan. §3 below.

Axial (row) truncation — side view

The object extends past the covered slab in z (here one-sided, like SiC). Rays reaching the edge detector rows traverse slices above the recon slab — that data is locally unexplainable, and nothing else in the sinogram is touched. Artifact: flash + damped ringing confined to the truncated end; the interior is unaffected. Seen in: the SiC composite scan. §4 below.

The asymmetry matters for remediation: the radial case corrupts the whole volume through interior channels, so down-weighting edge channels cannot fix it — enlarging the support can. The axial case is local and mirrors the situation the split_sino_recon sine weight taper already handles at an artificial detector-row split, so there a zero-memory row taper is a credible alternative to padding.

2  Method

Each case builds the truth phantom on an enlarged recon grid attached to a model that shares the real (small) detector. Forward-projecting that grid through the real detector is the physical truncated measurement — no sinogram cropping or other surgery, so the data inconsistency is exactly the one a real scan produces. Reconstruction then runs on the default-shape model (what a user gets: recon width = detector FoV at iso, zero margin), one iteration at a time, with per-region error tracked against the aligned center crop of the truth phantom.

  • Geometry: cone beam, magnification 2, 128 views over 2π, 40 iterations, default reconstruction parameters, unit weights.
  • Variants: default (auto recon shape) vs padded (scale_recon_shape, support enlarged to cover the object; recon compared on the same cropped voxels).
  • Regions: interior (r < 0.85 R, central slices), ring (0.85 R–R annulus inside the RoR), end slices (top / bottom slabs). NRMSE is normalized by the truth RMS over the RoR cylinder, so values are comparable across regions.

3  Radial (lateral) truncation — the ring

Phantom: a cylinder of radius 1.25× the FoV radius (contained in z), with three embedded spheres. Default grid (128, 128, 32); truth grid (172, 172, 32); padded variant ×1.35 laterally → (172, 172, 32).

Variant (iter 40)interior NRMSEring NRMSEring excess (signed)
default0.2252.21+0.028
padded ×1.350.0810.060+0.0004

Takeaway. Material outside the FoV projects onto interior channels too (a point at radius r crosses every channel |c| ≤ r as views rotate), so the inconsistency is spread across the sinogram and the whole interior pays. A channel weight taper can only address the edge channels — it cannot reach the interior bias — while support padding attacks the cause and fixes both. For the lateral case the open question is only the padding cost knee (memory ~scale²), not whether it is the right lever.

4  Axial truncation, one-sided — flash + z-ringing (the SiC case)

Phantom: a laminated cylinder (radius 0.75× FoV, alternating ±20% layers, one embedded sphere) whose bottom ends inside the covered slab but whose top extends 60% of a half-slab beyond it — like the SiC composite, which stays inside the FoV in channels but leaves the detector in rows. Default grid (96, 96, 64); truth grid (96, 96, 116); padded variant ×1.7 in z → (96, 96, 108).

Variant (iter 40)interior NRMSEtruncated-end NRMSEcontained-end NRMSE
default0.04720.6190.0433
padded ×1.7 in z0.04640.0710.0435

Takeaway. Unlike the lateral case, the axial artifact is local: the interior is untouched, and only the rows/slices near the truncated end are involved. That makes it exactly the situation the split_sino_recon sine taper already handles at an artificial split — so a geometry-derived row taper (zero memory cost) is a credible competitor to z-padding here, which is what Phase 2 should measure. Note also that z-slices are the cheap padding axis, so even the padding option is inexpensive for this case.

5  Implications for Phase 2

  • Padding is the standard to beat in both axes. Any weight-taper candidate must be A/B'd against scale_recon_shape on the same case.
  • Channels: taper cannot fix the interior bias (mechanism, confirmed visually); the useful sweep is the padding scale knee — how much support is enough, versus its ~scale² memory cost. A data-adaptive truncation detector (edge-channel sinogram level above the air floor) could auto-select the scale.
  • Rows: A/B a geometry-derived sine row taper (per the split_sino_recon precedent; taper the rows whose rays exit the recon slab) against z-padding: quality vs memory. One-sided handling matters (SiC truncates one side).
  • Stop-metric interaction: in the axial case the flash region is what keeps converging (slowly) while it also drags the change-% metric — remediation should both improve quality and let the 0.2% stop fire honestly.
  • Caveat: the "slower convergence" field observation only partially reproduced on these simple phantoms (damage was mostly a fast-reached bias floor). Watch for it on structured/real data in Phase 3 (SiC, z62, BGA).

6  Reproduction

Scripts: plans/experiments/flash_remediation/lateral_truncation_repro.py and z_truncation_repro.py (shared machinery in truncation_common.py); all knobs at the top of each script, no CLI args. Each runs in a few minutes on local CPU in the mbirjax conda env and writes these figures to figures/ plus metrics/recons to results/. Figures in this page are embedded (the repo gitignores PNGs).
